  rather than replaced: the same fundamental control vocabulary, the same twenty-four by
  eighty default, but faster, smaller, and considerably less expensive to put on a desk.

  What the VT320 did add was mostly a matter of capacity and correctness. It answered DECSCL
  at conformance level 3, one step above the VT220, and it supported ISO 8859-1 alongside
  DEC's own Multinational Character Set — a quiet but consequential concession that the wider
  industry, not DEC, would decide how accented characters were encoded. It carried multiple
  pages of screen memory, so a host could compose a form on an off-screen page and flip to it
  instantly rather than repainting line by line, and it offered several page lengths beyond
  the traditional twenty-four lines. The LK201 keyboard carried over, later joined by the
  LK401 with its additional modifier and Compose keys.

  The VT420 of 1990 is the more interesting machine technically, because it is where DEC
  added features that modern terminal emulators are still catching up with. The headline
  addition was rectangular area operations: a family of sequences that treat a bounded box of
  cells as a single object. DECCRA copies a rectangle from one part of the screen to
  another, DECFRA fills one with a given character, DECERA and DECSERA erase one, and DECCARA
  and DECRARA change or invert video attributes across one without touching the characters
  underneath. On a 9600-baud serial line these were enormously valuable — scrolling a
  sub-window or highlighting a block became a handful of bytes instead of a full repaint —
  and they anticipate, in hardware, exactly the operations a windowing text application
  performs constantly.

  Alongside them came horizontal margins. The VT100 had given applications a top and bottom
  scrolling margin through DECSTBM, which is why fixed headers and status bars are trivial to
  implement; the VT420 completed the picture with DECSLRM, left and right margins enabled
  through the DECLRMM mode. With both sets of margins in force, a program could define a
  genuine rectangular sub-window that scrolled independently of everything around it —
  side-by-side panes, each moving on its own, without the host redrawing a single unaffected
  cell. It is a striking capability to find in a 1990 serial terminal, and it went largely
  unused for decades because by the time anyone cared, people were writing for emulators that
  had not implemented it.

  The VT420 also supported two concurrent host sessions multiplexed over a single physical
  line, presented as a horizontally split screen, and it retained and extended the page
